traditions.name: Touch Montaigne's Shoe
traditions.description: Across the rue des Écoles from the Sorbonne, students touch the foot of Paul Landowski's seated Montaigne statue for luck before exams. Visitors can stop by the statue and see the shoe polished bright by generations of hands.

traditions.name: Richelieu's Cardinal Hat
traditions.description: In the Sorbonne Chapel, a cardinal's hat hangs above Cardinal Richelieu's marble tomb, as tradition dictates. Visitors can see it when the chapel opens for guided tours and Heritage Days.

traditions.name: Heritage Days at the Sorbonne
traditions.description: Each September during the European Heritage Days, the Sorbonne opens its reception halls and Grand Amphitheatre to the public for free. Visitors can walk up onto the amphitheatre's stage and tour rooms that are normally closed.

details.airportInfo: Charles de Gaulle is the main international gateway to Paris. RER line B runs from the airport into the city and stops at Luxembourg, a short walk from the Sorbonne.
details.funFact: The Sorbonne takes its name from the College of Sorbonne, founded around 1253 by Robert de Sorbon. Today's building is a late-19th-century reconstruction, but Cardinal Richelieu's domed chapel from the 1600s still stands in its courtyard.
details.languageInfo: French is the language of lectures and daily life. The Latin Quarter got its name from the Latin once spoken by the university's medieval scholars.
details.transportationFact: The Latin Quarter is compact and easy to walk. Cluny–La Sorbonne metro station and Luxembourg RER station are both a few minutes from the Sorbonne.

buildings.name: The Sorbonne
buildings.description: The building that gave the University of Paris its nickname has housed scholars since the College of Sorbonne opened here in 1253. Henri-Paul Nénot's grand reconstruction wraps a ceremonial courtyard, a peristyle and the Grand Amphitheatre, all still shared by the university's successor institutions.
buildings.oldUse: College of Sorbonne / University of Paris
buildings.newUse: Shared seat of the University of Paris's successor universities

buildings.name: Sorbonne Chapel
buildings.description: Jacques Lemercier designed this domed chapel for Cardinal Richelieu's rebuilding of the College of Sorbonne, and Richelieu's tomb lies beneath the dome. It is the only building left from that 17th-century campus; the rest was replaced in the 1800s.
buildings.newUse: Historic chapel (mostly closed since a 1999 storm)

buildings.name: Sainte-Geneviève Library
buildings.description: Henri Labrouste's reading room is a landmark of iron architecture: sixteen slender cast-iron Ionic columns carry openwork iron arches beneath twin barrel vaults. Facing the Panthéon, it is the main inter-university library of the universities of Paris.
buildings.oldUse: Library of the Abbey of Saint Genevieve's collection

buildings.name: École de Médecine
buildings.description: Built as the Academy of Surgery, Jacques Gondouin's building was the home of the Faculty of Medicine of Paris from 1795 to 1971. It even gave the street its name: Rue des Cordeliers became Rue de l'École-de-Médecine.
buildings.oldUse: Academy of Surgery / Faculty of Medicine
buildings.newUse: Head office of Paris Cité University

buildings.wiki: University of Paris Faculty of Law
buildings.name: Faculty of Law of Paris
buildings.description: Louis XV ordered a new home for the law faculty on the Place du Panthéon, and Jacques-Germain Soufflot, the Panthéon's own architect and a former law student here, designed it. It opened in 1774 and still serves law students today.
buildings.oldUse: Faculty of Law of the University of Paris

traditions.name: Galileo's Lectern
traditions.description: The wooden lectern Galileo is said to have lectured from, built for him by his own students according to tradition, stands at the entrance of the Sala dei Quaranta in Palazzo Bo. Visitors can see it on a guided tour of the palace.

traditions.name: Don't Jump the Chain
traditions.description: Local superstition holds that students should never jump over the chain in front of Palazzo Bo, or their studies will suffer. Visitors can see the chain and step around it.

traditions.name: Caffè Pedrocchi
traditions.description: The historic café beside Palazzo Bo has been a meeting place for students and professors since 1831, and students may sit in its green room without buying anything. Visitors can stop for its mint coffee and look for the bullet hole left from the 1848 student uprising in the white room.

details.nickname: Home of the first permanent anatomical theatre
details.airportInfo: Venice Marco Polo is the nearest major airport. From there, buses and trains via Venice Mestre reach Padua.
details.funFact: The University of Padua has had its seat in the Palazzo del Bo since 1493, and inside it is the world's first permanent anatomical theatre, a model copied by universities across Europe.
details.languageInfo: Italian is the language of the city and of most teaching at the university.
details.transportationFact: The university's historic buildings are spread through Padua's old centre, so walking is the easiest way to see them. Trams and buses cover the longer hops.

buildings.name: Anatomical Theatre of Padua
buildings.description: Inaugurated in 1595 by Girolamo Fabrici of Acquapendente, this is the first permanent anatomical theatre in the world. It became the model for the anatomical theatres built at Europe's main universities in the 17th century.
buildings.newUse: Historic theatre in the Palazzo del Bo

buildings.name: Orto botanico di Padova
buildings.description: Founded in 1545, this is the world's oldest academic botanical garden still in its original place. Its plan is a perfect square inside an 84-metre circle, split into quarters by paths that point to the four compass directions. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

buildings.name: La Specola
buildings.description: A 14th-century castle tower that was turned into an astronomical observatory in 1767. Its lower observatory sits 16 metres up and its upper observatory 35 metres up, and the university used it until the 1930s.

buildings.name: Palazzo Maldura
buildings.description: This 16th-century palazzo was remodelled in 1769 by Giovan Battista Novello for the lawyer Andrea Maldura. Its rooms keep many frescoes, and today it houses the university's Department of Language Studies and Literature.

traditions.name: Fonske
traditions.description: Fons Sapientiae ('Fountain of Wisdom') is a statue of a student pouring wisdom into his head while reading, given to the city by the university for its 550th anniversary in 1975. Student societies dress it up for special occasions, and visitors can stop for a photo on Rector De Somerplein.

traditions.name: University Library Carillon
traditions.description: The University Library tower holds one of Europe's largest carillons, a memorial gift from American engineers, and its main bell rings every hour. On tower visits the carillonneur takes visitors up to hear a live concert from the front row.

traditions.name: Totem on Ladeuzeplein
traditions.description: For its 575th anniversary in 2004, the university gave the city Jan Fabre's Totem, a giant jewel beetle stuck on a 23 m steel needle in front of the University Library. Visitors can take a photo of it on Ladeuzeplein.

details.airportInfo: Brussels Airport is the closest major airport. Direct trains run from the airport station to Leuven.
details.funFact: KU Leuven bought the whole Great Beguinage in 1962 and spent 25 years restoring it, so a historic quarter of almost 100 houses is now university housing and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
details.languageInfo: Leuven is in Flanders, so Dutch is the local language, though many master's programmes are taught in English. The motto over the University Hall door is Latin: 'Wisdom has built herself a house'.
details.transportationFact: Leuven's centre is small and the university is everywhere in it, so walking or cycling is the norm.

buildings.name: University Hall, Leuven
buildings.description: Begun in 1317 as Leuven's cloth hall, it became the heart of the university, with an upper floor added in the 1680s for teaching and the library. Burned in the Sack of Leuven in 1914 and restored in the 1920s, it is now KU Leuven's main administrative building.

buildings.name: KU Leuven University Library
buildings.description: After the old library in University Hall burned in 1914, American architect Whitney Warren designed this new one on the Ladeuzeplein. Built between 1921 and 1928, it is a showpiece of neo-Flemish Renaissance style.

buildings.name: Great Beguinage, Leuven
buildings.description: A whole medieval quarter of brick houses, canals and bridges, once home to communities of beguines. The university bought it in 1962 and restored it street by street under Professor Raymond Lemaire, and its early Gothic church is the widest in town.

buildings.name: Arenberg Castle
buildings.description: This brick-and-sandstone château, finished in 1515, was home to the Arenberg family until the First World War. The university acquired it in 1921, and it is now the main building of the Faculty of Engineering, with architecture studios inside.

traditions.name: Museum of Student Life
traditions.description: In a basement in the Otaniemi student village, the student union's museum (formerly the Polyteekkarimuseo) shows teekkari and other Aalto student traditions, from caps and overalls to famous pranks. Volunteer guides open it to visitors on Sunday afternoons during term.

traditions.name: Otaniemi Chapel Forest View
traditions.description: Heikki and Kaija Siren's 1956 campus chapel has a glass wall behind the altar that looks onto the forest and a cross set into the bedrock outside. The university lists the view as one of the most popular sights in Otaniemi.

details.airportInfo: Helsinki Airport is Finland's main international airport. From central Helsinki, the metro runs west to Aalto University station in Otaniemi.
details.funFact: Alvar Aalto designed the key buildings of the Otaniemi campus, including the main building and the library, and the campus is listed as national cultural heritage of Finland.
details.languageInfo: Espoo is officially bilingual, so signs appear in Finnish and Swedish (Otaniemi is Otnäs in Swedish). Much of the university's teaching is in English.
details.transportationFact: Aalto University metro station sits right in the middle of campus, connected to the Väre building. Light rail line 15 also stops at the Korkeakouluaukio square.

buildings.name: Aalto University Undergraduate Center
buildings.description: Alvar Aalto designed this as the main building of the Helsinki University of Technology. The first part was completed in 1965 and the extension with the major auditoriums followed in 1975.
buildings.oldUse: Main building of Helsinki University of Technology

buildings.name: Dipoli
buildings.description: Reima and Raili Pietilä's Dipoli is a celebrated work of expressionist modernism, opened in 1966. Built for the Helsinki University of Technology's Student Union, it was sold to Aalto University in 2014.

buildings.name: Väre
buildings.description: Home of the School of Arts, Design and Architecture, Väre won its design contest in 2013 and opened in 2018 with a metro station beneath it. It was one of Finland's nominees for the EU Mies van der Rohe Award in 2019.
buildings.oldUse: School of Arts, Design and Architecture
buildings.newUse: School of Arts, Design and Architecture

buildings.name: Harald Herlin Learning Centre
buildings.description: The campus library is another Alvar Aalto design, a four-storey building completed in 1969. Renovated from 2015, it is now the Harald Herlin Learning Centre.

traditions.name: Walpurgis Cap Raising
traditions.description: At 3 pm on 30 April, students on the slope below the Carolina Rediviva library put on their white student caps together as the rector waves his cap from the library balcony. Anyone can join the crowd on the hill to watch.

traditions.name: Spring Song at Gunillaklockan
traditions.description: On the evening of 30 April, students gather at the Gunilla bell beside Uppsala Castle for the spring song and the spring speech. Visitors can stand with the crowd and listen.

traditions.name: Gustavianum Anatomical Theatre
traditions.description: Under the copper cupola of the Gustavianum, the university museum preserves the anatomical theatre Olof Rudbeck the Elder built in the 1660s. Visitors can step inside it as part of a museum visit.

details.airportInfo: Arlanda, Stockholm's main airport, lies between Stockholm and Uppsala. Trains run from the airport north to Uppsala Central Station.
details.funFact: Carl Linnaeus owned the university's first botanical garden from 1741 and rearranged it to his own plan; it has been restored to look as it did in the 18th century.
details.languageInfo: Swedish is the local language, and many programmes are taught in English. Student life revolves around the 'nations', student societies named after regions of Sweden.
details.transportationFact: The historic university buildings cluster around the cathedral and University Park, all within a short walk of each other. Uppsala is also a famously bike-friendly city.

buildings.name: University Hall
buildings.description: Uppsala University's main building stands in University Park near the cathedral. Herman Teodor Holmgren designed it in an Italian Renaissance Beaux-Arts style, and it was completed in 1887.

buildings.name: Gustavianum
buildings.description: Built between 1622 and 1625, the Gustavianum is the oldest standing building of Uppsala University and was expanded by Olaus Rudbeck in 1662. It was the main university building from 1778 to 1887 and has been the university museum since 1997.
buildings.architect: Caspar van Panten; Olaus Rudbeck (1662 expansion)

buildings.name: Carolina Rediviva
buildings.description: Sweden's oldest and largest university library building was begun in 1820 and completed in 1841. It is where the Codex Argenteus, the 'Silver Bible', is kept.

buildings.name: Linnaean Garden
buildings.description: Olaus Rudbeck planted this garden in 1655, and Carl Linnaeus later owned it and rearranged it to his own design. Restored to his specifications, it is kept as an 18th-century botanical garden.

traditions.name: A Cabra, the Tower Bell
traditions.description: The best-known of the University Tower's four bells is nicknamed "a Cabra" (the goat), and it once called students to class. You can climb the tower's narrow stairs for a view over Coimbra and the Mondego River.

traditions.name: The Library Bats
traditions.description: Two colonies of small bats have lived in the Joanina Library for about two and a half centuries and eat the insects that would damage the books. Staff cover the tables with leather each evening to protect them.

traditions.name: Serenade on the Old Cathedral Steps
traditions.description: At midnight at the start of the Queima das Fitas in May, students sing Coimbra fado on the steps of the Old Cathedral. Thousands gather in the square to listen in silence.

details.airportInfo: Porto's Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport and Lisbon's Humberto Delgado Airport are the nearest major airports. From either city, trains on the Lisbon–Porto line stop at Coimbra-B station.
details.funFact: King Denis chartered the university in 1290, and it moved for good to Coimbra in 1537, into the old royal palace on top of the hill. The University of Coimbra – Alta and Sofia became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.
details.languageInfo: Portuguese is the language of classes and daily life. Latin was the official language of teaching until the university's reform in 1772, which is why the palace's long colonnaded balcony is called the Via Latina.
details.transportationFact: The old university sits at the top of a steep hill above the Baixa (lower town), so expect stairs and narrow streets. City buses climb to the upper town, and everything in the Alta is within walking distance.

buildings.name: Biblioteca Joanina
buildings.description: Built between 1717 and 1728 and named after King John V, this library is a showpiece of Portuguese Baroque. Its gilded shelves are decorated with Chinese motifs, and a 1725 portrait of the king hangs in the last room.

buildings.name: Chapel of São Miguel
buildings.description: This chapel of the old royal palace was planned by Marcos Pires from 1517 and finished by Diogo de Castilho after his death. Inside are tiled walls and a Baroque organ with nearly 2,000 pipes, a gift of King John V.

buildings.name: Coimbra University Tower
buildings.description: Italian architect António Canevari built the clock tower between 1728 and 1733, replacing an older tower. Its bells set the rhythm of university life, and visitors can now climb to the top.

buildings.name: Porta Férrea
buildings.description: Built in 1634, the Iron Gate was the first major work after the university bought the royal palace. António Tavares designed it as a two-sided triumphal arch with statues of King Denis and King John III.
buildings.newUse: Main entrance to the Paço das Escolas

buildings.name: University of Coimbra General Library
buildings.description: The university's main library opened its Edifício Novo in 1962, in buildings adapted from the old Faculty of Letters. It holds more than a million volumes and received the European Heritage Label in 2021.

buildings.name: Old Cathedral of Coimbra
buildings.description: Work on this fortress-like Romanesque cathedral gained momentum in 1162, and Sancho I was crowned here in 1185. Its steps are where students sing the midnight serenade that opens the Queima das Fitas.

traditions.name: Find the Frog
traditions.description: Hidden among the carvings of the university's Plateresque façade is a small frog sitting on a skull. Legend says a student who spots it will pass their exams, so visitors crowd the Patio de Escuelas searching for it.

traditions.name: The Sky of Salamanca
traditions.description: In the Escuelas Menores you can see Fernando Gallego's "Cielo de Salamanca", a painted sky of constellations and zodiac signs that once covered part of the vault of the old university library.

traditions.name: Spot the Vítores
traditions.description: Red monograms called vítores, made from the letters of the word "victor", are painted on university walls to honor people who earned a doctorate. Look for them around the Patio de Escuelas and the streets of the old town.

details.airportInfo: Madrid–Barajas is the main international gateway for Salamanca. From Madrid, trains and buses run west to Salamanca.
details.funFact: The University of Salamanca was founded in 1218 and is the oldest university in Spain still in operation. Its main building, the Escuelas Mayores, was finished in 1533 around a cloister next to the cathedrals.
details.languageInfo: Spanish is the language of classes and daily life, and Salamanca is one of Spain's most popular cities for learning it.
details.transportationFact: The old town is compact and largely pedestrian. The Plaza Mayor, the Casa de las Conchas, the Clerecía and the Patio de Escuelas are all a few minutes' walk apart.

buildings.name: Escuelas Mayores
buildings.description: The university's main building grew around a cloister from the early 1400s and was finished in 1533. Its Plateresque west façade, carved in the early 16th century, shows the Catholic Monarchs and is the most famous image of the university.
buildings.architect: Unknown (façade attributed to Juan de Talavera)

buildings.name: Colegio del Arzobispo Fonseca
buildings.description: Archbishop Alonso de Fonseca founded this college in 1519 for students from Galicia, and its building was finished in 1578 around a Renaissance cloister. It is the only one of Salamanca's old colegios mayores still standing, and its courtyard hosts summer concerts.
buildings.architect: Diego de Siloé; Rodrigo Gil de Hontañón; Juan de Álava
buildings.oldUse: Colegio Mayor de Santiago el Zebedeo

buildings.wiki: Colegio Mayor de San Bartolomé, Salamanca
buildings.name: Anaya Palace
buildings.description: After the 1755 Lisbon earthquake damaged the old Colegio de San Bartolomé, founded in 1401, this Neoclassical building replaced it from 1760. Its columned portico and grand staircase now lead to the Faculty of Philology.
buildings.architect: José de Hermosilla; Juan de Sagarvinaga

buildings.name: La Clerecía
buildings.description: Queen Margaret of Austria sponsored this huge Jesuit college, begun in 1617 and finished in 1754. Its Baroque towers rise over the old town, and the building is now the seat of the Pontifical University of Salamanca.
buildings.architect: Juan Gómez de Mora; Andrés García de Quiñones
buildings.oldUse: Real Colegio del Espíritu Santo (Jesuit college)

buildings.name: Casa de las Conchas
buildings.description: University professor Rodrigo Arias de Maldonado built this house between 1493 and 1517 and covered its façade with more than 300 scallop shells, the symbol of the Order of Santiago. It now houses a public library.
buildings.oldUse: Residence of Rodrigo Arias de Maldonado
